formats.name: Email
formats.summary: Short, clear and polite, with a subject line that says what it is about.
layout: To: the person's email address.
Subject: a few words that say what the email is about, such as "Volunteer application for Panda Week".
A greeting on its own line.
Short paragraphs, one main point each.
A sign-off and your name (in practice tasks, use a made-up name).
formats.opening: Say who you are and why you are writing in the first one or two sentences. For example: "I am writing to apply for a place as a Panda Week volunteer."
formats.closing: Say what you would like to happen next, then sign off. For example: "I look forward to hearing from you. Kind regards,"
formats.tone: If you don't know the person, keep it formal: "Dear Mr Patel", no slang, no text-speak, no emojis. If you know them well, you can be friendlier, but still use full sentences.
checklist: I included a subject line.
I started with a greeting, such as "Dear ...".
My first paragraph says why I am writing.
I used a new paragraph for each main point.
I ended with what I want to happen next.
I signed off, such as "Kind regards" and a name.

practice.prompt: You are emailing someone you have never met. Which opening is best?
options: Hiya! Hope ur well :)
Dear Mr Patel, I am writing to ask about volunteering at Panda Week.
To whoever reads this, I want to volunteer.
Hey Sam, quick question.
practice.why: It uses a formal greeting and says straight away why you are writing. The others are too casual for someone you don't know.

formats.name: Formal letter
formats.summary: Like a formal email, but with addresses and a date.
layout: Your address in the top right corner.
The date underneath your address.
The other person's name or job title and address on the left, a little lower.
A greeting: "Dear Ms Khan" if you know the name, "Dear Sir or Madam" if you don't.
Paragraphs, then a sign-off and your name.
formats.opening: State your purpose clearly: "I am writing to complain about ..." or "I am writing to ask for ..."
formats.closing: Use "Yours sincerely" if you used their name, and "Yours faithfully" if you wrote "Dear Sir or Madam".
formats.tone: Formal and polite, even when you are complaining. Explain calmly, give reasons, and suggest what should happen.
checklist: I included my address and the date.
I included the other person's name or job title and address.
My greeting and sign-off match (sincerely or faithfully).
My first paragraph says why I am writing.
I stayed polite throughout.

practice.prompt: You started your letter with "Dear Sir or Madam". How should you sign off?
options: Yours faithfully
Yours sincerely
Love from
Cheers
practice.why: When you don't know the person's name, you use "Yours faithfully". "Yours sincerely" goes with a named person, such as "Dear Ms Khan".

formats.name: Article
formats.summary: For a newsletter, magazine or website. It needs a headline and should grab the reader.
layout: A headline that is short and catches attention.
A subheading (optional) that adds a little more detail.
Paragraphs. You can use subheadings to break up a longer article.
Your name as the writer (a by-line) is optional.
formats.opening: Hook the reader. You could ask a question, give a surprising fact (from the task), or describe a scene. Then make it clear what the article is about.
formats.closing: End with a memorable final thought or a call to action, such as "So next Monday, leave the car at home and catch the bus."
formats.tone: Match the readers. For students you can be lively and direct ("you"), but keep it in full sentences without slang.
checklist: I wrote a headline.
My opening hooks the reader.
I used paragraphs, and subheadings if it is long.
I spoke to the reader directly where it helps.
I ended with a strong final thought or call to action.

practice.prompt: Which is the best headline for a college newsletter article encouraging students to use buses?
options: Buses
This article is about buses and why you should use them more often than you do now
bus
Get On Board: Why the Bus Beats the School Run
practice.why: It is short, catches attention and hints at the article's point. The others are too plain or too long.

formats.name: Review
formats.summary: Your opinion of something, with reasons, to help other people decide.
layout: A title that names what you are reviewing.
A star rating or score (optional).
Paragraphs: what it is, what was good, what was not so good.
A final recommendation.
formats.opening: Say what you are reviewing and give a quick first impression: "I visited Hollins Park with my family last weekend, and it was better than I expected."
formats.closing: Give a clear recommendation and who it would suit: "I'd recommend it to families with young children, but go early."
formats.tone: Friendly and honest. Give reasons and examples for every opinion, not just "it was good".
checklist: I named what I am reviewing.
I gave good points with reasons.
I gave at least one thing that could be better.
I ended with a clear recommendation.

practice.prompt: Which sentence would work best in a review?
options: It was good.
I went there.
The feeding talk was the highlight, because the keeper answered every question from the children.
Everything was bad and nobody should go.
practice.why: It gives an opinion and a reason with a specific example, which helps the reader decide.

formats.name: Report
formats.summary: Information and recommendations for a group, laid out in clear sections.
layout: A title that says what the report is about.
To, From and Date lines (optional, but useful).
An introduction that says why the report was written.
Subheadings for each section.
A final section called "Recommendations" or "Conclusion".
formats.opening: Explain the purpose: "This report looks at what there is for young people in Hawsden and Brayminster, and suggests ways to improve it."
formats.closing: Give clear recommendations. Numbered points work well: "1. Run a later bus on Fridays."
formats.tone: Formal and factual. Avoid "I think" in most of it. Save opinions for the recommendations, and explain them.
checklist: I gave the report a title.
My introduction explains the purpose.
I used subheadings for each section.
I kept the tone formal and factual.
I finished with clear recommendations.

practice.prompt: Which subheading suits a formal report?
options: Stuff that's rubbish
Transport
OMG the buses!!
so yeah
practice.why: Report subheadings should be short and plain, so the reader can find each section quickly.

formats.name: Blog post
formats.summary: A personal, chatty piece for a website, with a clear view.
layout: A title that catches attention.
Short paragraphs, which are easier to read on a screen.
Subheadings or a list are fine if they help.
formats.opening: Start in a personal way, such as a question or a short story, and make your view clear early on.
formats.closing: Sum up your view and invite readers to respond: "Where would you rather live? Let me know in the comments."
formats.tone: Personal and friendly ("I", "you"), but still in full sentences with accurate spelling and punctuation. No text-speak.
checklist: I wrote a title.
My opening is personal and makes my view clear.
I used short paragraphs.
I gave reasons for my view.
I ended by summing up or inviting a response.

practice.prompt: Which is the best final sentence for a blog post?
options: So that's why I'd pick a village every time. Would you? Tell me in the comments.
The end.
Bye.
That's all I have to say about towns and villages and stuff.
practice.why: It sums up the writer's view and invites the reader to respond, which suits a blog.

spag.name: Full stops and capital letters
explain: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (or a question mark or exclamation mark).
Use capital letters for names of people, places, days and months, and for "I".
If you have two complete sentences, don't join them with a comma. Use a full stop instead.

example.wrong: the bus was late, we missed the start.
example.right: The bus was late. We missed the start.

options: we went to tel aviv in may.
We went to tel aviv in may.
We went to Tel Aviv in may
We went to Tel Aviv in May.
practice.why: The sentence starts with a capital, "Tel Aviv" and "May" are names so they need capitals, and it ends with a full stop.

spag.name: Question marks
explain: Use a question mark at the end of a direct question.
Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why, how, can, could, do or is.
In emails and letters, questions are a good way to ask for information politely.

example.wrong: Could you tell me what time the talk starts.
example.right: Could you tell me what time the talk starts?

practice.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark at the end?
options: I would like to book two tickets
The bus leaves at ten
Is lunch included in the price
Please send me a timetable
practice.why: "Is lunch included in the price" is asking something, so it ends with a question mark.

spag.name: Exclamation marks
explain: Use an exclamation mark to show strong feeling, surprise or a command.
Use only one at a time, and not too often. In formal writing, you may not need any.
They work well in an article or a blog: "Leave the car at home!"

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses an exclamation mark best?
options: Dear Sir or Madam!
I am writing to ask about tickets!
Try the bus for one week and see the difference!
Yours faithfully!
practice.why: This is a call to action in a persuasive piece, so an exclamation mark adds energy. The others are formal phrases that should not have one.

spag.name: Commas
explain: Use commas to separate items in a list: "falafel, hummus and salad". You usually don't need one before "and".
Use a comma after an opening word or phrase: "However, the bus was late." "In the morning, we went to the market."
Don't use a comma to join two full sentences.

example.wrong: We saw pandas monkeys and meerkats.
example.right: We saw pandas, monkeys and meerkats.

options: After lunch, we walked to the beach.
After lunch we, walked to the beach.
After, lunch we walked to the beach.
After lunch we walked, to the beach.
practice.why: "After lunch" is an opening phrase, so the comma goes straight after it.

spag.name: Apostrophes for belonging
explain: Use an apostrophe to show something belongs to someone: "the keeper's talk" (one keeper).
If the owner is a plural ending in s, put the apostrophe after the s: "the pandas' enclosure" (more than one panda).
Plurals that don't own anything don't need an apostrophe: "two pandas", not "two panda's".

options: The bus's were all late.
The drivers seat was broken.
The driver's seat was broken.
The drivers' seat's was broken.
practice.why: The seat belongs to one driver, so it is "driver's". "Buses" is just a plural, so it never needs an apostrophe.

spag.name: Apostrophes for missing letters
explain: An apostrophe can show where letters have been left out: "don't" (do not), "we're" (we are), "it's" (it is).
"Its" without an apostrophe means "belonging to it": "The bus changed its route."
In formal writing, such as a report or a formal letter, it is often better to write the full words: "do not" instead of "don't".

example.wrong: Its a long walk and the hill has it's own bus stop.
example.right: It's a long walk and the hill has its own bus stop.

options: The council changed it's mind.
Its going to rain later.
It's going to rain later.
The village has it's own shop.
practice.why: "It's going to rain" means "it is going to rain", so it needs the apostrophe. In the other sentences, "its" means "belonging to it" and should have no apostrophe.

spag.name: Inverted commas (speech marks)
explain: Put inverted commas around the exact words someone said: The keeper said, "Pandas like a quiet space."
The punctuation at the end of the spoken words goes inside the inverted commas.
You can also use inverted commas around a short quotation or a title: the council calls it "a better route".

example.wrong: The driver said "next stop, Station Road".
example.right: The driver said, "Next stop, Station Road."

options: My friend said, "The train is quicker."
My friend said "the train is quicker".
My friend said, The train is "quicker."
"My friend said", the train is quicker.
practice.why: There is a comma before the speech, the spoken words start with a capital letter, and the full stop goes inside the inverted commas.

spag.name: Words that sound the same
explain: "There" is a place (over there). "Their" means belonging to them. "They're" means they are.
"Your" means belonging to you. "You're" means you are.
"To" is for direction (to the bus stop). "Too" means also or very (too late). "Two" is the number 2.

example.wrong: Their going too the station at to o'clock.
example.right: They're going to the station at two o'clock.

options: Your going to love the food.
Youre going to love the food.
Your' going to love the food.
You're going to love the food.
practice.why: "You're" is short for "you are": "You are going to love the food."

spag.name: Grammar: was or were, and staying in one tense
explain: Use "was" with I, he, she and it. Use "were" with we, you and they: "We were late."
Pick a tense and stick to it. If you start in the past ("we went"), keep going in the past ("we saw", not "we see").
Write "should have" or "could have", not "should of" or "could of".

example.wrong: We was on the train and then we see the sea.
example.right: We were on the train and then we saw the sea.

options: The buses was all full.
We should of left earlier.
They were waiting at the stop.
Yesterday we go to the park.
practice.why: "They" goes with "were". The others mix up was and were, use "should of" instead of "should have", or use the wrong tense for yesterday.
